query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Alloying NbMoTaW with a minor addition (~5 atomic %) of titanium will enhance its room‐temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while preserving the high-temperature BCC structural stability and strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal‐atomic, single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW, which exhibits excellent mechanical performance at temperatures up to 1600 °C but shows limited ductility at room temperature and uncertain experimental irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 atomic % titanium into the NbMoTaW alloy formulation while rebalancing the remaining elemental concentrations to retain a refractory HEA composition.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests at room temperature for ductility evaluation, high-temperature tests up to 1600 °C for strength and creep assessment, and controlled helium ion irradiation experiments under reactor‐relevant fluences and energies.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized lattice distortions and the formation of nanoscale heterogeneities within the BCC matrix that act both as dislocation mobility enhancers and as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
generation.mechanism: Titanium incorporation reduces the effective energy barrier for dislocation movement by inducing lattice distortions, thereby increasing ductility. Simultaneously, the heterogeneous lattice environment facilitates the recombination of irradiation-induced defects, mitigating damage while preserving the high-temperature stability of the BCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to undoped NbMoTaW, the Ti-doped alloy is expected to exhibit noticeably improved room-temperature ductility (e.g., greater strain-to-fracture) and reduced irradiation-induced defect accumulation, with minimal impact on its high-temperature strength and creep resistance.
generation.baseline: Undoped, equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW alloy known for its high-temperature strength but limited room-temperature ductility and unverified irradiation behavior.
generation.boundary: The expected enhancements are anticipated across a service temperature range from ambient (for ductility and irradiation performance) up to 1600 °C, under helium ion irradiation conditions representative of reactor environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of ductility improvement and reduction in defect accumulation under irradiation remains to be quantified, and care must be taken to ensure that excessive titanium does not promote unwanted secondary phase formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the baseline equiatomic NbMoTaW and (2) NbMoTaW alloyed with ~5 atomic % Ti. Confirm phase retention using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Evaluate room-temperature tensile ductility, high-temperature mechanical performance (up to 1600 °C), and subject samples to helium ion irradiation under controlled conditions to assess defect density and blister formation.
measurements: XRD and TEM for phase and microstructural verification
Room-temperature tensile tests (strain-to-failure, yield stress)
High-temperature yield strength and creep tests
Post-irradiation analysis via TEM/SEM for defect density and blistering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped NbMoTaW does not show statistically significant improvements in room-temperature ductility and irradiation resistance (i.e., similar or higher defect densities) without a marked loss in high-temperature performance compared to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. Refractory HEAs (RHEAs) stand out among various types of HEAs due to their unparalleled mechanical properties at high temperatures exceeding 800 °C, and even up to 1500 °C in some cases [,], making them viable options for high-temperature structural applications, outperforming typical Ni-based superalloys. Refractory high-entropy alloys, thanks to their high strength at high temperatures, high melting point, and high hardness brought by their resistance to friction and wear properties, may be used in aerospace engines, gas turbines, and the nuclear irradiation field. However, the reported literature has primarily centered on compression deformation investigations. For most RHEAs, due to their room-temperature brittleness, their tensile ductility is commonly negligible []. Therefore, improving the room-temperature plasticity of RHEAs is the premise of its high-temperature application.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown promising potential applications in advanced reactors due to the outstanding mechanical properties and irradiation tolerance at elevated temperatures. In this work, the novel low-activation Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 HEAs were designed and prepared to explore high-performance HEAs under irradiation. The microstructures and mechanical properties of the Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 HEAs before and after irradiation were investigated. The results showed that the unirradiated Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 HEAs displayed a single-phase BCC structure. The yield strength of the Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 HEAs increased gradually with the increase of Hf content without decreasing the plasticity at room and elevated temperatures. After irradiation, no obvious radiation-induced segregations or precipitations were found in the transmission electron microscope results of the representative Ti2ZrHfV0.5Ta0.2 HEA. drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor concentration of a ductilizing element such as titanium to NbMoTaW will improve room‐temperature ductility and irradiation resistance while preserving the BCC high‐temperature mechanical performance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW, which exhibits excellent high-temperature strength (up to 1600 °C) but poor room-temperature ductility and unverified irradiation tolerance.
drafts.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 atomic % of titanium into the NbMoTaW alloy, adjusting the balance of the other elements to maintain an overall refractory HEA composition.
drafts.conditions: Testing is to be performed at room temperature for ductility and under controlled irradiation conditions (e.g., helium implantation with energy ranges known to cause blistering and defect formation) as well as at high temperatures up to 1600 °C for mechanical performance.
drafts.structural_mediator: The addition of titanium is expected to induce localized lattice distortions within the BCC matrix that lower the effective Peierls barrier and provide additional heterogeneous interfaces acting as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
drafts.mechanism: Titanium reduces the energy barrier for dislocation movement by distorting the lattice, thereby enhancing dislocation mobility and increasing ductility at room temperature. At the same time, the resultant lattice heterogeneity and interface density serve to trap and recombine irradiation-induced defects, reducing amorphization and precipitation under irradiation, all while maintaining the high-temperature BCC phase.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-doped alloy is predicted to show significantly improved room-temperature ductility (e.g., higher strain-to-fracture) and enhanced irradiation tolerance (i.e., lower defect accumulation and reduced phase instability) without a marked loss in high-temperature strength and creep resistance up to 1600 °C.
drafts.baseline: Properties of equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW, with known high-temperature strength but limited room-temperature ductility and uncertain irradiation behavior.
drafts.boundary: The improvements are expected within the temperature range from room temperature up to 1600 °C and under irradiation regimes typical of helium implantation experiments that simulate service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two alloy variants: (1) baseline equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW and (2) NbMoTaW with 5 atomic % Ti substitution. Characterize both alloys through XRD and TEM to confirm retention of the BCC structure. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to assess ductility, high-temperature mechanical tests (up to 1600 °C) to evaluate strength, and controlled helium implantation experiments to observe irradiation effects (e.g., defect density, blistering, or amorphization).
measurements: XRD and TEM for phase and microstructural analysis
Room-temperature strain-to-fracture and tensile strength
High-temperature mechanical performance (strength, yield stress, creep tests)
Post-irradiation defect density and extent of amorphization via TEM
Surface analysis for blistering or irradiation-induced precipitation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and reduced irradiation-induced defects, or if its high-temperature performance degrades relative to baseline NbMoTaW, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Partial substitution of NbMoTaW with a ductility‐promoting element (e.g., ~5–10 at.% vanadium) will enhance room‐temperature ductility and irradiation-induced defect recombination while retaining the high-temperature BCC phase stability and strength of the base NbMoTaW alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW known for excellent high-temperature strength (up to 1600 °C) but poor ductility at room temperature, with only computational indications of irradiation tolerance.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate a small concentration (approximately 5–10 atomic percent) of vanadium into the NbMoTaW alloy to form a NbMoTaW-V solid solution.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical testing at room temperature for ductility, high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) mechanical tests for strength retention, and controlled irradiation (e.g., helium implantation at energies where blistering and defect accumulation are concerns) to evaluate irradiation resistance.
drafts.structural_mediator: Modified dislocation behavior and enhanced defect recombination mediated by changes in local lattice bonding and atomic spacing due to vanadium incorporation, which may also promote dynamic recovery under irradiation.
drafts.mechanism: Vanadium addition is expected to reduce the yield strength at room temperature by enabling easier dislocation motion and increased grain-boundary sliding, leading to enhanced ductility. Simultaneously, the altered lattice environment can facilitate the mobility and recombination of irradiation-induced defects, improving irradiation tolerance without disrupting the high-temperature BCC phase stability.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The V-doped NbMoTaW alloy should exhibit noticeably improved tensile ductility at room temperature and lower irradiation-induced defect accumulation compared to the undoped alloy, while maintaining comparable high-temperature strength and phase stability up to 1600 °C.
drafts.baseline: Undoped, equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW alloy with excellent high-temperature strength but poor ductility and uncertain experimental irradiation response.
drafts.boundary: The improvements are expected to apply under ambient to moderate service temperatures (including room temperature for ductility and up to 1600 °C for high-temperature performance) and under irradiation conditions relevant to helium implantation studies where the alloy is subjected to moderate blistering and defect accumulation.

Use TEM and XRD for post-irradiation structural and phase stability analyses.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile strain to failure and yield stress
High-temperature (up to 1600 °C) compressive/tensile strength measurements
Irradiation-induced defect density and blistering via TEM
Phase stability and precipitation behavior by XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vanadium-added NbMoTaW alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and a reduction in irradiation-induced defect accumulation, or if they exhibit compromised high-temperature strength or destabilized BCC phase (e.g., formation of secondary phases), then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (e.g., 5–10 at.%) of a ductility‐promoting element such as Cr or V to the equiatomic single-phase BCC NbMoTaW will promote the formation of a controlled dual-phase microstructure (a primary BCC matrix with dispersed nanoscale ductile phase or coherent precipitates) that improves room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance without sacrificing high-temperature strength.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW with excellent mechanical strength at high temperatures (up to 1600 °C) but poor ductility at room temperature and uncertain experimental irradiation performance.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a small percentage of a ductile element (e.g., Cr or V) into the NbMoTaW alloy composition, targeting ~5–10 at.% addition relative to the base elements.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical testing at room temperature for ductility evaluation, high-temperature testing (up to 1600 °C) for strength retention, and helium ion irradiation experiments under reactor-relevant conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure in which the primary BCC matrix retains high-temperature stability and the secondary nanoscale ductile phase (or coherent precipitates) serves as defect sinks and facilitates dislocation activity at lower temperatures.
drafts.mechanism: Minor alloying induces localized lattice distortions that favor a fine-scale, dual-phase structure. This structure both improves dislocation mobility at room temperature (enhancing ductility) and provides additional sinks for irradiation-induced defects, thereby promoting defect recombination and self-healing while maintaining the BCC matrix that imparts high-temperature strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to show increased room-temperature tensile ductility and enhanced resistance to irradiation (reduced helium bubble formation and irradiation hardening) while preserving the high yield strength observed in pure NbMoTaW at ultrahigh temperatures.
drafts.baseline: Unmodified equiatomic NbMoTaW, noted for its excellent high-temperature mechanical performance but limited room-temperature ductility and uncertain irradiation resistance.
drafts.boundary: The benefits are anticipated under service temperatures below approximately 800 °C for ductility improvements and up to 1600 °C for retaining high-temperature strength, as well as under helium ion irradiation conditions typical of reactor environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples—(i) the baseline equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW and (ii) NbMoTaW with 5–10 at.% Cr (or V) addition. Process both sets under identical conditions and characterize their microstructures to confirm the presence of a controlled dual-phase structure in the modified alloy. Subject both sets to room-temperature tensile tests, high-temperature yield strength tests (up to 1600 °C), and helium ion irradiation experiments at reactor-relevant fluences.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile elongation and ductility
High-temperature yield strength and stress–strain behavior
Irradiation-induced hardening (e.g., via nanoindentation) and defect characterization (using TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy with Cr (or V) addition does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and/or irradiation resistance compared to the baseline NbMoTaW (or if it compromises high-temperature strength), the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount (e.g., 2–5 at.%) of an HCP‐stabilizing element such as Ti into equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW will induce a dual-phase microstructure that improves room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while maintaining high-temperature structural stability and strength.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW that exhibits substantial high-temperature strength but very low ductility at room temperature and only computationally predicted irradiation resistance.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of a ductility‐enhancing, HCP‐stabilizing element (e.g., Ti) into the NbMoTaW formulation to form a microstructure with a dominant BCC phase and dispersed nano-scale HCP precipitates.
drafts.conditions: Testing over a temperature range from room temperature to 1600 °C and under irradiation conditions (e.g., helium ion implantation) representative of reactor environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale HCP precipitates within the BCC matrix, which can increase active slip systems at room temperature and serve as sinks for irradiation‐induced defects.
drafts.mechanism: The HCP precipitates enable enhanced dislocation motion and activate additional plasticity mechanisms at lower temperatures, while their interfaces with the BCC matrix encourage recombination of irradiation-induced defects, thereby reducing hardening and defect accumulation. At high temperatures, the dominant BCC phase ensures that the excellent strength and thermal stability are preserved.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-alloyed variant should show significantly improved ductility and reduced irradiation-induced hardening/damage at room temperature, without a notable loss in high-temperature strength or phase stability.
drafts.baseline: Unmodified equiatomic NbMoTaW showing poor room-temperature ductility and only computationally assumed irradiation tolerance despite excellent high-temperature performance.
drafts.boundary: The improvements are expected to manifest under conditions typical of reactor operations, from room temperature up to 1600 °C, and under irradiation doses and energies analogous to those encountered in fission or fusion environments.

Process both sets to ensure similar grain sizes and microstructural homogeneity. Subject samples to room-temperature tensile tests, high-temperature compression tests up to 1600 °C, and standardized helium ion irradiation under controlled fluence and temperature conditions.
measurements: Room-temperature ductility (e.g., elongation to failure)
High-temperature yield strength and stress-strain behavior
